text:
Something is happening right now that will shape the rest of your life.
And almost nobody around you is talking about it.
[pause]
The people building it are.
Last month, the head of one of the biggest AI labs wrote: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models."
He's asking to slow down. Not because it isn't working. Because it is.
In mathematics, problems that sat untouched for decades are falling.
In biology, AI is finding things no human has ever seen.
In public health, a report that took all day now takes under an hour.
[pause]
And the month isn't even over yet.

Most of us picture AI progress as a few big moments, with long quiet stretches in between.
So let's draw it. One line, and every first gets a card.
Nineteen fifty-six. A handful of scientists meet at Dartmouth for a summer, and give the field its name: artificial intelligence.
Then, for decades, almost nothing you could see.
Forty-one years later, in nineteen ninety-seven, a computer beats the world chess champion.
Fifteen years after that, a neural network learns to recognise what's in a photo, far better than anything before it.
Four years: AlphaGo beats one of the best Go players alive.
Four years: AlphaFold cracks how proteins fold, a fifty-year-old puzzle in biology.
Two years: ChatGPT.
Four months: GPT-4 scores high enough to pass the bar exam.
[pause]
Decades. Then years. Then months.
Watch one field. In July twenty twenty-five, AI reaches gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad, the hardest contest for students on Earth.
Ten months later, it disproves a conjecture that had stood for eighty years. Nine outside mathematicians check the proof. It holds.
The Fields Medal winner Tim Gowers: "No previous AI-generated proof has come close to that."
[pause]
The gaps between the cards are shrinking. And the people closest to it say so in plain words: "The rate at which AI models improve is accelerating."
Over the last three months, the gaps shrank to days.

August first. OpenAI publishes ten results in mathematics.
Ten problems where nobody had made progress in at least a decade. One bound in sphere packing hadn't moved since nineteen seventy-eight.
An unreleased model found the arguments, then checked every step in a proof language a computer can verify.
The computing bill, by OpenAI's estimate: about two thousand dollars.
None of it is peer-reviewed yet. And a month later, an even bigger claim, about the Navier-Stokes equations, ran into a wall of mathematicians saying: not so fast.
Keep that in mind. Checking is going to matter.

Twenty-five days.
August twenty-sixth. Nvidia reports eighty-nine billion dollars in data-center sales. In three months. More than double a year before.
Its finance chief expects the five biggest cloud companies to spend about one point three trillion dollars next year, much of it on this.
On the same call, its CEO, Jensen Huang: "AI has reached its inflection point."
That's the fuel. Every card on this line runs on it.

Seventeen days.
September twelfth. The head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, publishes an essay. He doesn't ask to stop. He asks to slow the pace a little.
That's the essay from the beginning.

Ten days.
September twenty-second. An engineer leaves a new AI model working overnight, across six codebases. In the morning, it's still going. More than eighteen hours, on one task.
That model costs forty percent less than the one before it. Which came out in July.

One day.
September twenty-third. Nine hundred and fifty AI agents search the DNA of living things, for twenty-one hours.
One of them stops at a strange pattern, and writes a note: "I can see by eye a tandem repeat array... a CRISPR-like repeat array?!"
It's a system no one had described before. Scientists check it in the lab. It's real.
That's the discovery from the beginning.
Feng Zhang, one of the pioneers of CRISPR gene editing: "This is an exciting example of how AI agents can contribute to biological discovery."

And then the cards start landing on top of each other.
September twenty-sixth. America and China agree to open a channel for AI incidents.
Twenty-ninth. The US government starts officially calling the technology "Super Intelligence".
Thirtieth. Google ships its most capable model.
October twelfth. Meta does the same.
Four of the biggest labs, flagship models, inside four weeks.

So why are the cards coming faster?
Because each one makes the next one cheaper.
The best model of a few months ago gets cheaper by half, or more, every few months.
Cheap enough, and you don't run one agent. You run nine hundred and fifty.
More attempts mean more finds. More finds bring more money. More money buys more chips.
It's a loop. And loops are what bend a curve.
[pause]
But here's what keeps this honest.
Google checked whether its AI is speeding up its own research. AI already writes most of Google's new code. Yet it found no significant speed-up in the research itself. Not yet.
The loop is turning. It isn't closed.
And not everyone thinks the world will feel it quickly. Two Princeton researchers argue the big effects on society will be slow, "on the timescale of decades."
An economist who studies this answers: "Steam, electricity, and computers each gave societies decades to adapt. AI may give us only a few years."
Both could be right, about different things. The capability is moving in weeks. How fast it changes our lives is still partly up to us.

So here's the question this curve puts to us.
In September, Sam Altman told the UN Security Council the choice is between "a new Renaissance of creativity and discovery" and "a new Industrial Revolution of upheaval and disarray."
When firsts arrive every few days, we can do what we've always done. Wait for each one to prove itself, then react.
Or we can build the checking, the referees and the phone lines now, while it's calm, and decide where to point the pace.
[pause]
Pause here. Which would you choose?

Let's imagine it's twenty twenty-nine. Just a scenario.
An epidemiologist in Kinshasa named Amani opens her laptop on the first morning of a new outbreak.
In one version, we waited.
The tools got faster every month. Nobody built the checks.
Her inbox fills with AI reports. Some brilliant, some wrong, and she can't tell which.
So she trusts none of them, and does it all by hand.
[pause]
Same morning. Same outbreak. The other version.
Every model that reaches her was tested by people outside the company that built it.
The virus genome is assembled before lunch. The case map updates by the hour.
She isn't working less. She's working on today, not last week.
[pause]
Same curve in both. Same speed. The difference is what we built around it.

First, referees inside the building.
On October fifteenth, Anthropic gave six evaluators from METR, an independent research group, access to its hardware, offices and internal tools, close to what its own safety teams get.
In the company's words: "Anthropic can't veto publication."
It's the first concrete step from Amodei's essay. Outside eyes before a model ships, not after.
It's voluntary. It's one company. Six people can't see everything.
But the company also wrote: "we believe every frontier AI company should do the same." A standard like that can become law.

Second, a phone line.
In nineteen sixty-three, after the Cuban Missile Crisis, Washington and Moscow set up a direct line, so a misunderstanding wouldn't turn into a war.
On September twenty-sixth, the United States and China agreed to a channel for AI incidents.
Coverage called the summit short on breakthroughs. The real talks start in November. A channel isn't a treaty.
But when things move in days, the cheapest safety tool of all is knowing who to call.

Third, check everything.
Remember the math? Those ten results came with proofs a computer can verify, line by line.
And the Navier-Stokes claim? Mathematicians took it apart in public, within weeks.
That isn't the system failing. That's the system working.
In July, more than eleven hundred people at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta signed a letter asking the government for tools to slow things down, if it ever becomes necessary.
The builders are asking for brakes they hope they'll never need.
Checking costs time and money. It's the one thing the curve won't hand us for free.

Fourth, point the curve at the right problems.
This September, health workers fighting Ebola in Congo used AI to build their daily situation report. A report that used to take all day to put together can now take under an hour.
The virologist Jean-Jacques Muyembe: "You beat Ebola by knowing where it is today, not where it was last week."
That didn't happen by itself. Someone chose the problem.
Cheap intelligence flows toward whatever pays. Unless public health, schools and science get in line first, with the money to match.

Back to our line of cards.
The gaps between the cards keep getting shorter. That part, we don't control.
The gap we do control is the one between a new card and our response.
So next time an AI headline stops you, ask two things. Who checked it? And when was the last one like it?
And if you want to do more, ask the people who represent you to make outside testing a rule, not a favour.
[pause]
Somewhere on this line, maybe a few months from now, is a card you've been waiting for. A cure. An answer.
[softly] Let's make sure we're ready to trust it.
[pause]
What's the last AI headline that made you stop? Tell me in the comments.
